items.title: MLB: Steering an American legend toward the future without abandoning its past
items.summary: Mother Design's own case study of its two-and-a-half-year rebrand of Major League Baseball, built on five custom typefaces from different type designers (a Franklin Gothic revival, a condensed Clarendon slab, a classic script, an octagonal 'ballpark signage' face and a hand-lettered one), each reviving lettering from the sport's history.
items.why: Its two-axis chart (how close a product sits to the game, how much fans expect) decides how plain or expressive each sub-brand's design gets, plain for the ticketing app and loud for social: a principled way for CueDesign to let MathGym be playful while tutoring and parent screens stay calm, inside one system.

items.title: EdTech Can Work. Decision Makers Have to Check the Evidence First.
items.summary: Sal Khan walks through the independent, randomised trials behind well-known learning products (Khan Academy, ASSISTments, India's Mindspark, Carnegie Learning) and explains how to read them, using yardsticks like 'standard deviations' of learning gain, where intensive one-on-one tutoring typically scores 0.2 to 0.4.
items.why: It's the lens schools and informed parents will use to judge Cuemath, and two numbers are product-strategy inputs: the strongest results came from roughly 30 to 60 minutes of use per student per week, and Mindspark, an Indian after-school math program, gained 0.37 in math in under five months, a concrete target for how much practice MathGym's motivation loop should drive.

items.title: Studio Kiln builds a shape-shifting character for weight loss app Reset
items.summary: Studio Kiln designed Ester, the mascot for weight-loss app Reset: a faceless figure made of soft 3D blocks that shows how it 'feels' only by tumbling apart and reassembling (no smiles or frowns), with a different colour version for each of the app's five user types.
items.why: A worked alternative to the cartoon smile-or-frown mascot most kids' apps use for right and wrong answers: emotion carried purely by motion, so learners project their own feelings instead of being judged by a face, plus one character recoloured per user type, a pattern that could flex across Cuemath's belts or levels.

items.title: Design Creativity Bench: Measuring creativity in LLM-Generated UI
items.summary: A study from AI design-tool maker Kombai that gave leading AI models and human designers the same interface briefs: every model met over 90% of the brief's requirements, but different models' designs looked more like each other than like a human's, and when asked for the same kind of screen for two different products, the AI changed its design far less than people did.
items.why: Hard numbers for how Cuemath's team should use AI screen generators: trust them to hit the brief, but expect same-y output (creative range 0.58 for AI versus 0.90 for humans), so distinctiveness has to come from your own direction and references; worth knowing the authors sell a tool that claims to fix this.

items.title: Nobody learns good taste by being told
items.summary: Designer Tobias van Schneider argues taste can be taught, but not by declaring things good or bad: show people better references side by side, let them spot the difference themselves, explain the reasoning behind your calls, and hand them real decisions to defend.
items.why: A ready routine for a design lead growing a team's eye: swap 'this isn't working' crits for side-by-side comparisons, which matters more now that AI makes competent-but-generic screens cheap (see the study above) and judgement is the scarce skill.
